pr-what.label: supported
pr-what.says: Dionysiou Areopagitou Street is a pedestrian street beside the south slope of the Acropolis.
quote: is a pedestrianized street, adjacent to the south slope of the Acropolis in the Makrygianni district of Athens

pr-name.label: supported
pr-name.says: It is named after Dionysius the Areopagite, who according to Acts was the first Athenian convert after Paul's sermon, and is the patron saint of Athens.
quote: It is named after Dionysius the Areopagite, the first Athenian convert to Christianity after Apostle Paul's sermon, according to the Acts of the Apostles, and patron saint of the city of Athens.

pr-route.label: supported
pr-route.says: The street runs east to west, from Amalias Avenue near the Arch of Hadrian to near Philopappos Hill, where it continues as Apostolou Pavlou.
quote: The street runs from east to west. It starts from Amalias Avenue near the Arch of Hadrian and ends near Philopappos Hill where it continues as Apostolou Pavlou Avenue, the rest of the pedestrian zone which goes around the archaeological site of the Acropolis and the Agora.

pr-views.label: supported
pr-views.says: The route gives views of the Parthenon and the Agora, away from the busy center.
quote: The entire route provides visitors with views of the Parthenon and the Agora (the meeting point of ancient Athenians), away from the busy city centre.

pr-pikionis.label: supported
pr-pikionis.says: It took its present shape in 1955, redesigned by the architect Dimitris Pikionis, who also designed the paved paths of the archaeological site; it was fully pedestrianized in 2003.
quote: It acquired its current shape in 1955, when it was redesigned by architect Dimitris Pikionis, who also designed the paved paths of the archaeological site. The street was finally pedestrianized in 2003.

pr-1857.label: supported
pr-1857.says: The street was first mapped in 1857, further north than today, next to the Odeon of Herodes Atticus.
quote: The street was first mapped in 1857 in a position more northern than where it is located today, adjacently to the Odeon of Herodes Atticus.

pr-olympics.label: supported
pr-olympics.says: For the 2004 Olympics Athens linked its ancient sites with a network of pedestrian streets, the Unification of Archaeological Sites.
quote: Athens hosted the 2004 Summer Olympic Games.
the Unification of Archaeological Sites (which connects the city's classical-era ruins and monuments to each other through a network of pleasant pedestrianized streets)

pr-north.label: supported
pr-north.says: After Makrygianni Street the buildings stop on the north side and the archaeological site begins; near there is the entrance to the Theatre of Dionysus.
quote: after Makrygianni Street, buildings cease on the north side and give place to the archaeological site of the Acropolis. Near Makrygianni Street is the entrance to the ancient Theatre of Dionysus.

pr-south.label: supported
pr-south.says: On the south side is the Acropolis Museum; near the end is the entrance to the Odeon of Herodes Atticus; the foundations of the house of Proclus were found in the middle of the street.
quote: On the south side is the Acropolis Museum and an upmarket residential district with apartment buildings and houses. Near the end is the entrance to the Odeon of Herodes Atticus. In the middle of the street were found the foundations of the house of Proclus.

pr-vangelis.label: supported
pr-vangelis.says: The composer Vangelis owned a neoclassical mansion near the Acropolis Museum.
quote: Vangelis Papathanasiou, composer. He owned a neoclassical mansion near the Acropolis Museum

pr-heat.label: supported
pr-heat.says: In summer it is very hot: drink enough water and use sunscreen.
quote: In the summer, the weather is very hot. Remember to drink enough water and apply sunscreen to your skin.

pr-walk.label: supported

quote: A mostly car-free archaeological walk starts at Vasilisis Amalias Street, passes in front of the Acropolis Museum, Acropolis, Herodion Theatre, Thiseio (Apostolou Pavlou Str), Ermou Street and ends at the popular area of Kerameikos

parts.name: The start of the walk
parts.stand: At the eastern end of the street, near Amalias Avenue and the Arch of Hadrian, facing west along the car-free street.

paras.t: This is Dionysiou Areopagitou Street, the walking street that runs along the south slope of the Acropolis. From here it heads west, all the way to Philopappos Hill, and along the way you get views up to the Acropolis and the Parthenon.
In summer this walk gets very hot. Carry water, drink enough of it, and put on sunscreen.
The street got its present shape in 1955, from the architect Dimitris Pikionis. He also designed the paved paths up on the archaeological site. Cars were finally taken off it in 2003.

For the 2004 Olympics, Athens joined up its ancient sites with a network of walking streets. Today a mostly car-free walk runs from here, past the Acropolis Museum and the Odeon, all the way to Kerameikos.

parts.name: Who the street is named for
parts.stand: Keep walking west, and pause anywhere you can see the Acropolis rock on your right.

paras.t: The street's name takes you back to the Bible. The street is named after Dionysius the Areopagite. The book of Acts tells how the apostle Paul spoke to the Athenians, and Dionysius was among those who believed.

Here are the words, from Acts chapter seventeen, in the King James Version: Howbeit certain men clave unto him, and believed: among the which was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
That's Scripture. What came later is the Church's memory of him: today Dionysius is the patron saint of Athens.

parts.name: Along the slope
parts.stand: Past Makrygianni Street, where the buildings on your right stop and the slope of the Acropolis begins.

paras.t: Notice how the houses on the right have stopped. From here on, that side of the street belongs to the archaeological site. Near here is the entrance to the Theatre of Dionysus, and across the street, on your left, is the Acropolis Museum.
A small detail along the way: near the Acropolis Museum, the composer Vangelis owned a neoclassical mansion.

parts.name: Toward Philopappos Hill
parts.stand: Near the western end, by the entrance to the Odeon of Herodes Atticus.

paras.t: Here, near the end, is the entrance to the Odeon of Herodes Atticus. When the street was first mapped, in 1857, it actually ran further north, right beside the Odeon.
Ahead, the street ends near Philopappos Hill. The walking route carries on as Apostolou Pavlou, around the Acropolis and the Agora.

So the man this street is named after was one listener who said yes. Of all the people who heard Paul in Athens, his is the name you've been walking on. One person who listened, remembered by a whole city.
